course.title: Blockchain & Cryptocurrency
course.description: A plain-language, non-promotional tour of how blockchains and cryptocurrencies actually work, from distributed ledgers and cryptographic hashing to consensus, smart contracts, and the real limitations and risks. Structure and framing are adapted from the open overview on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), with original prose and worked examples throughout. The aim is clear understanding and sober judgment, not investment advice or hype.

questions.prompt: A blockchain is best described as
options: a central database owned and controlled by one company
a distributed, append-only ledger shared across many computers
a kind of web browser for secure sites
a single encrypted file stored on one server
questions.explanation: A blockchain is a shared ledger copied across many participants that only grows by appending new records - see 'What a blockchain is'.

questions.prompt: A cryptographic hash function takes an input and produces
options: a fixed-size fingerprint that changes completely if the input changes
a reversible code you can decode straight back to the input
a random number that has nothing to do with the input
a compressed copy of the input that you can unzip later
questions.explanation: A hash is a fixed-size, one-way fingerprint; a tiny input change flips the output completely.

questions.prompt: Blocks are linked into a chain because each block stores
options: the hash of the previous block
the phone number of the miner who made it
a full copy of every other block
nothing at all about other blocks
questions.explanation: Each block embeds the previous block's hash, so the blocks are chained together.

questions.prompt: In public-key cryptography, you share your ... and keep your ... secret
options: private key; public key
public key; private key
username; password
wallet; ledger
questions.explanation: The public key can be shared freely; the private key must stay secret because it authorizes spending.

options: one master server controls all the others
computers connect directly as equals with no central controller
only banks are allowed to run the software
all the data lives in a single location
questions.explanation: Peer-to-peer means computers connect directly as equals, with no central hub in charge.

questions.prompt: Proof of work secures a blockchain by requiring participants to
options: spend real-world computing effort to add a block
show a government-issued identity document
pay a monthly subscription fee
vote for one another by email
questions.explanation: Proof of work makes adding a block costly in computation, so cheating is more expensive than honesty.

questions.prompt: Proof of stake chooses who adds the next block based mainly on
options: who solves a numerical puzzle fastest
coins a participant locks up as a deposit
alphabetical order of usernames
which computer on the network is oldest
questions.explanation: Proof of stake selects validators roughly in proportion to the deposit, or stake, they lock up.

questions.prompt: Which statement about blockchains is accurate?
options: any transaction can be instantly reversed by an administrator
once confirmed and buried under later blocks, records are very hard to change
every design uses almost no energy
they are completely immune to scams and fraud
questions.explanation: Deep records are practically immutable, but blockchains are not energy-free, administrator-reversible, or fraud-proof.

lessons.title: What a blockchain is, and the problem it solves
lessons.grammar_note: Append-only means you can add new entries but never rewrite old ones; it does not mean the ledger is secret.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain in plain language what a blockchain is and the specific problem it was built to address. By the end of this lesson you will be able to define a ledger, say why the words distributed and append-only matter, and describe the double-spending problem that ordinary digital money runs into without a trusted middleman. You will also be able to state, in a sentence or two, how keeping many identical copies of a record can stand in for trust in a single central authority. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in your own words, what is a distributed, append-only ledger, and who holds the copies? Keep that answer in mind, because the rest of the lesson builds directly on it. We will stay concrete and skip the hype. A blockchain is a data structure plus a set of rules, not magic. It fits some problems well and other problems poorly, and knowing which is which is the real skill.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A ledger is simply a record of who owns what and which transactions have happened, like a bank's list of account balances. In most systems one organization keeps the ledger, and everyone trusts it to be honest and available. A blockchain removes that single keeper. Instead, many computers each store a full copy of the ledger, and they follow shared rules to agree on new entries. The ledger is append-only: new records are added to the end, and past records are not edited or deleted. Records are grouped into blocks, and each block is linked to the one before it, forming a chain. The problem this solves is double spending. A digital coin is just data, and data can be copied, so without a central referee a person could try to spend the same coin twice by sending two conflicting messages. A central bank prevents this by being the single authority on balances. A blockchain prevents it instead by having the whole network agree on one shared history, so only one of two conflicting transactions can be accepted.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Picture a shared spreadsheet that thousands of people each hold an identical copy of. Nobody can quietly change a past row, because everyone else still has the original and would notice the mismatch. To add a row, the network runs an agreement procedure so that all honest copies end up the same. Example: Alice has 5 coins and tries to send 5 coins to Bob and the same 5 coins to Carol at the same instant. On a single bank ledger the bank simply rejects the second request. On a blockchain, the network collects pending transactions, agrees on an order, and includes only one of the two; the other is dropped as invalid because the coins are already spent. Another example: a public blockchain lets anyone read the full history and check balances for themselves, rather than asking a company to vouch for them. This openness is a feature for some uses, such as auditing, and a drawback for others, such as private medical data, which does not belong on a public, permanent record.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what does append-only mean? 2) Name the problem a blockchain solves that plain digital files cannot solve alone. 3) True or false: on a public blockchain, only the owner can read the transaction history. 4) Why does keeping many copies of the ledger make tampering harder? 5) Give one kind of data that should not go on a public blockchain. Answers: 1) New records are only added to the end; existing records are not changed or removed. 2) Double spending - stopping the same coin from being spent twice without a central referee. 3) False; on a public blockchain anyone can read the history, though identities are usually pseudonymous. 4) Any change to a past record would disagree with the many honest copies, so the network rejects it. 5) Private or sensitive personal data, such as medical records, because the ledger is permanent and widely visible.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a blockchain is a single file stored in one place. It is a shared, replicated record held by many computers at once. Mistake: assuming blockchains are anonymous. Most public ones are pseudonymous, meaning your real name is hidden behind an address, but every transaction tied to that address is visible forever, and analysis can sometimes link addresses back to people. Mistake: believing a blockchain is always the right tool. When one trusted party can keep the records cheaply, an ordinary database is simpler, faster, and greener. Exit ticket: (a) What two properties are captured by the words distributed and append-only? (b) What is double spending? Answers: distributed means many parties each hold a full copy; append-only means records are added but not edited or deleted. Double spending is the attempt to spend the same digital coin more than once, which a blockchain prevents by making the whole network agree on a single shared history.

lessons.title: Cryptographic hashing and how blocks chain together
lessons.grammar_note: A hash is a one-way fingerprint: easy to compute forward, but practically impossible to reverse back to the original input.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe what a cryptographic hash function does and explain how hashes link blocks into a tamper-evident chain. By the end you will be able to list the key properties of a good hash function, show why changing one block breaks every block after it, and explain the role of the previous-block hash stored inside each block. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that each block stores the hash of the block before it. Why would that single design choice make it obvious if someone edited an old block? Hold on to your guess. This lesson keeps things concrete with small, made-up hashes so you can see the mechanism, even though real hash outputs are long strings of hexadecimal digits. The goal is intuition about why the chain is hard to rewrite, not memorizing any particular algorithm. You do not need advanced math to follow along; you only need to track how one value feeds into the next.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A cryptographic hash function takes any input - a word, a file, or a whole block - and returns a fixed-size string called a hash or digest. Good hash functions have three properties that matter here. First, the same input always gives the same output, so anyone can recompute and check it. Second, even a tiny change to the input, such as flipping one letter, produces a completely different, unpredictable output; this is called the avalanche effect. Third, the function is one-way: given a hash, you cannot practically work backward to find the input, and you cannot easily find two different inputs that share the same hash. Now the chaining trick. Each block contains its transactions plus the hash of the previous block. That previous hash is part of the current block's own data, so it is included when the current block's hash is computed. This means every block's hash depends on the entire history before it. Edit any old block and its hash changes, which changes the next block's stored previous hash, which changes that block's hash, and so on down the line.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Here is a toy illustration using short fake hashes. Block 1 holds some data and hashes to A1. Block 2 stores Block 1's hash (A1) plus its own data, and the whole thing hashes to B2. Block 3 stores B2 plus its data and hashes to C3. Now suppose an attacker edits Block 1 to steal coins. Block 1 now hashes to something new, say Z9, instead of A1. But Block 2 still records the old value A1 as its previous hash, so the chain no longer matches: Block 2 points to a block that no longer exists in that form. To cover the trail, the attacker must recompute Block 2, which changes B2, which forces recomputing Block 3, and every block after it. On a busy network with many honest copies and, as later lessons show, deliberately costly block creation, redoing the entire chain faster than everyone else is wildly impractical. That is why editing buried history is so hard: the cost is not editing one block but redoing all the blocks that follow it, everywhere at once.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three hash properties from this lesson. 2) What is the avalanche effect? 3) In the toy example, if Block 1 is edited, why does Block 2 no longer line up? 4) Can you take a hash and compute the original input from it? 5) Why does editing an old block force an attacker to redo later blocks too? Answers: 1) Deterministic (same input gives the same output), avalanche (a small change gives a totally different output), and one-way (you cannot reverse it or easily find collisions). 2) A tiny change to the input flips the output completely and unpredictably. 3) Block 2 still stores the old previous hash, which no longer matches the edited Block 1's new hash. 4) No; a cryptographic hash is practically impossible to reverse. 5) Each block's hash depends on the previous block's hash, so changing one block changes every hash that follows.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing hashing with encryption. Encryption is reversible with a key so you can recover the message; hashing is one-way and is used to verify integrity, not to hide and later reveal data. Mistake: thinking a hash stores the data in compressed form. A hash is a fixed-size fingerprint and throws information away, so you cannot rebuild the input from it. Mistake: assuming two different files could never share a hash. Collisions are possible in theory, but a strong hash function makes finding them so hard that we treat matching hashes as proof the inputs match. Exit ticket: (a) What does each block store that links it to the one before it? (b) Why does editing an old block invalidate the blocks after it? Answers: each block stores the previous block's hash as part of its own data; editing an old block changes its hash, so the next block's stored previous hash no longer matches, and the mismatch cascades forward through the whole chain.

lessons.title: Public-key cryptography, wallets, and digital signatures
lessons.grammar_note: Your public key is like an account number you can share; your private key is like the pen that signs for it, and it must stay secret.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how public-key cryptography lets someone prove they authorized a transaction without revealing a secret, and describe what a wallet actually holds. By the end you will be able to distinguish a public key from a private key, explain what a digital signature proves, and say why losing a private key means losing access to the funds. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you matched public keys to sharing and private keys to secrecy. Why can a signature made with a private key be checked by anyone holding only the matching public key? Keep that question open. We will avoid heavy math and focus on what each piece does and why it keeps control of funds in the right hands. A wallet, you will see, is less like a purse that holds coins and more like a keychain that holds the keys which prove ownership of coins recorded on the ledger. Getting this mental model right prevents a lot of expensive mistakes later.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Public-key cryptography gives each user a pair of mathematically linked keys: a public key, which can be shared freely, and a private key, which must be kept secret. The pair has a special relationship. A message signed with the private key can be verified by anyone using the matching public key, yet knowing the public key does not let anyone work out the private key. On a blockchain, an address is derived from a public key, and it works like an account identifier that people can send funds to. To spend funds sitting at that address, you create a digital signature with the corresponding private key. The network checks the signature against the public key and confirms two things: the transaction was authorized by the private-key holder, and the transaction has not been altered since it was signed. A wallet is software or hardware that stores your private keys and helps you sign transactions. It does not hold coins directly; the coins are entries on the shared ledger, and the keys are what prove you may move them.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example: Alice wants to send 2 coins to Bob. Her wallet builds a transaction that says, in effect, move 2 coins from Alice's address to Bob's address, and signs it with Alice's private key. She broadcasts the signed transaction. Every node can verify, using Alice's public key, that the signature is valid and that nobody changed the amount or the recipient along the way. Nobody needs Alice's private key to check this; the public key is enough. Because only Alice's private key could have produced that signature, she cannot later deny sending it, and an impostor cannot forge it. This is why key management matters so much. If you lose your private key, there is no password reset and no help desk that can recover it, so the funds become permanently inaccessible. If someone steals your private key, they can sign transactions as you and drain the address. Hardware wallets keep keys on a dedicated device to reduce this risk, and some people split backups across safe locations, but the core rule stands: whoever controls the private key controls the funds.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which key do you share, and which do you keep secret? 2) What two things does verifying a digital signature prove? 3) Does checking a signature require the signer's private key? 4) What does a wallet actually store? 5) What happens if you lose your private key with no backup? Answers: 1) Share the public key; keep the private key secret. 2) That the holder of the private key authorized the transaction, and that the transaction was not changed after signing. 3) No; verification uses only the public key. 4) It stores your private keys, and helps you sign, rather than the coins themselves, which live on the ledger. 5) The funds at that address become permanently inaccessible, since there is no recovery mechanism.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing the wallet holds your coins like a physical purse. The coins are ledger entries; the wallet holds the keys that authorize moving them. Mistake: sharing or screenshotting a private key or its recovery phrase. Anyone who sees it gains full control, so treat it like the only key to a vault. Mistake: thinking a forgotten key can be reset. Unlike a bank password, there is usually no authority that can restore access, which is the price of removing the central keeper. Mistake: assuming a public address reveals your identity. It is pseudonymous, though activity tied to it is public and sometimes traceable. Exit ticket: (a) What does a digital signature let the network confirm? (b) Why is protecting the private key the whole game? Answers: a signature confirms the rightful key holder authorized an unaltered transaction; protecting the private key is essential because whoever holds it can sign transactions and move the funds, with no reset available if it is lost or stolen.

questions.prompt: A blockchain is best described as
options: a private file on a single server
a distributed, append-only ledger copied across many computers
a faster kind of email
a company that stores passwords
questions.explanation: Many computers each hold a full copy of an append-only ledger and agree on its contents.

questions.prompt: The core problem a blockchain is designed to solve is
options: slow internet speeds
double spending without a central referee
weak phone batteries
spelling errors in documents
questions.explanation: A blockchain stops the same digital coin from being spent twice without trusting a central authority.

options: reversible if you have the right key
one-way, turning any input into a fixed-size fingerprint
a way to compress files you can unzip later
a random number that ignores the input
questions.explanation: A hash is a one-way, fixed-size fingerprint of its input; you cannot reverse it to recover the input.

questions.prompt: Blocks are chained together because each block stores
options: the hash of the previous block
a backup of every user's password
the current time and nothing else
a full copy of the next block
questions.explanation: Embedding the previous block's hash makes each block depend on all the history before it.

questions.prompt: If an attacker edits a block buried deep in the chain, they must
options: do nothing, since other blocks are unaffected
recompute that block and every block after it
simply email the other nodes
change a single character one time
questions.explanation: Editing one block changes its hash, which forces recomputing every block stacked on top of it.

questions.prompt: To spend funds held at an address, you must
options: publish your private key to the network
sign the transaction with the matching private key
ask a central bank for approval
share your recovery phrase with a node
questions.explanation: Only a signature made with the matching private key authorizes spending; the key itself stays secret.

lessons.title: Decentralization, peer-to-peer networks, and consensus
lessons.grammar_note: A node is any computer running the network's software and keeping a copy of the ledger; a miner or validator is a node that also competes or is chosen to add new blocks.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a blockchain network is organized without a central server and explain, at a high level, how many independent computers agree on one shared history. By the end you will be able to define a node, explain what peer-to-peer means, and compare two common consensus mechanisms: proof of work and proof of stake. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you identified a peer-to-peer network as computers connecting directly as equals. If no one is in charge, what stops two honest computers from recording different versions of events? That gap - agreeing on a single order of transactions among parties who do not trust each other - is exactly what consensus mechanisms close. We will keep the comparison balanced: each approach has real strengths and real costs, and neither is free. By the end you should be able to explain the basic trade-offs in your own words rather than treating either one as obviously best.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In a peer-to-peer network, computers connect directly as equals rather than through a central hub. Each participant runs software and can keep a full copy of the ledger; such a computer is called a node. Nodes share new transactions and new blocks with their neighbors, who pass them along, so information spreads across the whole network without a central coordinator. Decentralization means no single party controls the ledger or can unilaterally change the rules. The hard part is consensus: getting many mutually distrustful nodes to agree on the same ordered history, even when some are offline, slow, or dishonest. A consensus mechanism is the rulebook for choosing who gets to add the next block and how everyone else checks it. Proof of work and proof of stake are two widely used answers. Both aim to make cheating expensive and honesty cheap to verify, so that following the rules is the most profitable strategy. The difference lies in what resource you must commit to earn the right to add a block: real computing effort, or value you lock up as a stake.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Proof of work, used by Bitcoin, asks participants called miners to repeatedly try numbers until one finds a value that makes the block's hash fall below a target. This takes enormous trial-and-error computation, which costs electricity and hardware. The winner proposes the next block and earns a reward; everyone else can check the answer instantly. Cheating would mean out-computing the entire honest network, which is extremely costly. The well-known downside is high energy use. Proof of stake, used by Ethereum since 2022 and by many newer networks, instead asks participants called validators to lock up a deposit of the network's own coins. The protocol then chooses validators to propose and confirm blocks, roughly in proportion to their stake. A validator who tries to cheat can have part of their deposit destroyed, a penalty called slashing. This uses far less energy, but critics worry it can concentrate influence among those who already hold the most coins. Both designs replace trust in a person with an incentive: behaving honestly pays, and attacking the network is meant to cost more than it could ever gain.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a node? 2) In one sentence, what problem does a consensus mechanism solve? 3) What resource must you commit under proof of work? 4) What resource must you commit under proof of stake? 5) Name one drawback often raised about each mechanism. Answers: 1) A computer running the network's software, usually keeping a full copy of the ledger. 2) It gets many distrustful computers to agree on a single, ordered history and on who may add the next block. 3) Real computing effort, which costs electricity and hardware. 4) A deposit of the network's coins, locked up as a stake. 5) Proof of work is criticized for heavy energy use; proof of stake is criticized for possibly concentrating influence among the largest coin holders.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking decentralized means there are no rules. There are strict rules; what is missing is a single party with the power to override them. Mistake: assuming every node mines or validates. Many nodes simply store and relay the ledger and check that incoming blocks follow the rules, without competing to create blocks. Mistake: treating proof of work and proof of stake as good versus bad. Each trades off energy, security assumptions, and how power is distributed, and reasonable people weigh those trade-offs differently. Mistake: believing decentralization is all-or-nothing. In practice networks sit on a spectrum, and some are far more concentrated than their marketing suggests. Exit ticket: (a) What does a consensus mechanism accomplish? (b) Give the core difference between proof of work and proof of stake. Answers: a consensus mechanism lets untrusting nodes agree on one ordered history and on who adds the next block; proof of work commits computing effort to earn that right, while proof of stake commits a locked deposit of coins.

lessons.title: Bitcoin: how a transaction works, mining, and forks
lessons.grammar_note: Confirmations count how many blocks have been added on top of the block that contains your transaction; more confirmations mean the transaction is harder to reverse.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Walk through what happens, step by step, when someone sends Bitcoin, and explain mining, forks, and why old transactions become effectively permanent. By the end you will be able to trace a transaction from signing to confirmation, say what miners are paid for, and explain what a fork is and why not every fork is a crisis. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that buried records are very hard to change. After this lesson you should be able to explain what buries them and why more blocks on top mean more safety. Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first widely used blockchain, so it is a useful concrete example even if you never intend to use it. We will describe how it works mechanically and leave aside whether it is a good investment, which is a separate question touched on later and well outside the scope of this lesson.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sending Bitcoin follows a clear sequence. First, your wallet builds a transaction that specifies the amount and the recipient's address, then signs it with your private key. Second, your wallet broadcasts the signed transaction to the peer-to-peer network, where nodes check that your signature is valid and that you actually have the funds. Valid transactions wait in a pool of pending transactions. Third, miners gather pending transactions into a candidate block and compete, through proof of work, to find the number that makes the block valid. Fourth, the winning miner broadcasts the new block; other nodes verify it and add it to their copy of the chain. Your transaction is now confirmed once, and each later block stacked on top adds another confirmation. Miners are paid in two ways: a block reward of newly created coins, and the transaction fees attached to the transactions they include. The block reward shrinks over time in scheduled steps called halvings, which is how Bitcoin limits its total supply to a fixed cap. This issuance schedule is fixed in the rules, not set by any central bank.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Confirmations matter because of how forks work. Occasionally two miners find valid blocks at nearly the same moment, so the network briefly sees two competing chain tips; this is a natural, temporary fork. Nodes follow the rule of building on the chain with the most accumulated work, so within a block or two one branch wins and the other is abandoned, along with its block. Transactions in the abandoned block usually return to the pending pool and get included later. This is why merchants wait for several confirmations before treating a large payment as final: the deeper a transaction is buried, the more work an attacker would have to redo to reverse it. A different kind of fork is a protocol change. A soft fork tightens the rules in a backward-compatible way, while a hard fork changes the rules so that old software rejects the new blocks, which can split a network into two separate chains, as happened when Bitcoin Cash split from Bitcoin in 2017. So forks range from routine and self-healing to deliberate and permanent, and the word alone does not tell you which.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does your wallet do before broadcasting a transaction? 2) What are miners paid, and from what two sources? 3) What is a confirmation? 4) Why do merchants wait for several confirmations on large payments? 5) What is the difference between a temporary fork and a hard fork? Answers: 1) It builds the transaction and signs it with your private key. 2) They are paid in newly created coins (the block reward) plus the transaction fees of the transactions they include. 3) A confirmation is a block added on top of the block containing your transaction; the first inclusion is one confirmation, and each later block adds one more. 4) More confirmations mean more accumulated work sits on top, so reversing the transaction becomes impractical. 5) A temporary fork is two blocks found at once, resolved quickly by following the chain with the most work; a hard fork is a rule change that can permanently split the network into two chains.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a transaction is final the instant you send it. It is only pending until a miner includes it in a block, and it grows safer as confirmations accumulate. Mistake: believing miners decide balances by hand. Miners only order and bundle valid transactions; the rules, checked by every node, decide what is valid. Mistake: assuming immutability is absolute. In principle a transaction could be reversed by redoing more work than the rest of the network combined, but in practice this is so costly for a large, healthy chain that we treat deep history as permanent. Mistake: hearing fork and assuming disaster. Most forks are routine and heal in moments. Exit ticket: (a) List the four steps of a Bitcoin transaction from signing to confirmation. (b) Why does immutability get stronger over time? Answers: sign, broadcast and validate, bundle into a block through mining, then verify and append; immutability strengthens because each added block piles more work on top, making any reversal progressively harder.

lessons.title: Ethereum, smart contracts, and tokens
lessons.grammar_note: A token is a record of ownership managed by a smart contract; a fungible token is interchangeable like a coin, while a non-fungible token is unique like a numbered ticket.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how Ethereum extends the blockchain idea from moving money to running programs, and describe what smart contracts and tokens are. By the end you will be able to say what a smart contract does, distinguish fungible from non-fungible tokens, and give a balanced account of both the promise and the pitfalls. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that confirmed records are hard to change. If code runs on such a ledger and cannot easily be edited after launch, what does that imply about bugs in that code? Hold that thought, because it explains why smart-contract security is a serious and recurring problem. Ethereum, launched in 2015, is the most widely used programmable blockchain, so it makes a good example, but the concepts apply to many networks. As always, we will describe how these tools work and where they fail, without recommending that you buy, build, or invest in anything.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Bitcoin mainly records transfers of one coin. Ethereum generalizes this by running small programs, called smart contracts, directly on the blockchain. A smart contract is code stored on the ledger that executes exactly as written when triggered by a transaction, with its results recorded on the chain. Because every node runs the same code and checks the same result, no single party can secretly alter the outcome. The phrase smart contract is a bit misleading: it is neither smart nor a legal contract, just deterministic code that moves value and data according to its rules. Contracts are what make tokens possible. A token is an entry, managed by a contract, that represents ownership of something. Fungible tokens are interchangeable units, like currency, where one unit equals any other; common standards let projects issue their own coin-like tokens. Non-fungible tokens are unique records that point to a specific item, such as a particular piece of art or a ticket, where each token is distinct and not interchangeable. Running a contract costs a fee, often called gas, paid to compensate the network for the computation.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Example of a smart contract: an escrow that holds funds and releases them to a seller only after a buyer confirms delivery, or refunds the buyer after a deadline. Once deployed, it follows its own rules automatically, with no bank in the middle. Example of fungible tokens: a project issues a token where every unit is identical and divisible, useful for things like in-app credits or representing a share of a pool. Example of non-fungible tokens: a digital artwork is linked to a single token whose ownership history is public; buying the token records you as the current holder, though in many cases the token points to the item rather than storing the item itself, and the underlying file may live elsewhere. The key caution is that immutability cuts both ways. If a contract has a bug, that bug is also hard to change, and attackers have drained large sums from flawed contracts. Likewise, owning a non-fungible token records ownership of the token, which is not the same as holding copyright or guaranteeing the linked file will exist forever. Read what a token actually grants before assuming it grants more.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In plain terms, what is a smart contract? 2) Why is the name smart contract somewhat misleading? 3) What is the difference between a fungible and a non-fungible token? 4) What is gas? 5) Why is a bug in a deployed contract especially dangerous? Answers: 1) Code stored on the blockchain that runs exactly as written when triggered, with results recorded on the chain. 2) It is not intelligent and is usually not a legal contract; it is just deterministic code that executes automatically. 3) Fungible tokens are interchangeable units like currency; non-fungible tokens are unique and not interchangeable, each pointing to a specific item. 4) A fee paid to the network to compensate it for running a contract's computation. 5) Because deployed code is hard to change, a bug can persist and be exploited, and the resulting losses can be large and irreversible.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a smart contract is safe simply because it is on a blockchain. The ledger faithfully runs whatever the code says, including its bugs, so the code must be audited carefully. Mistake: believing a non-fungible token stores the artwork. Usually the token stores a link or identifier, and the file lives elsewhere, which can break if that storage goes away. Mistake: thinking owning a token grants copyright or legal rights by default. It records ownership of the token itself; any further rights depend on separate terms. Mistake: treating all tokens as investments. Many have no cash flow behind them, and prices can be driven by hype, which connects to the risks covered in the next lesson. Exit ticket: (a) What does a smart contract do, and what can it not protect you from? (b) Give one real difference between fungible and non-fungible tokens. Answers: it runs code automatically on the ledger but cannot protect you from flaws in that code; fungible tokens are interchangeable units, while non-fungible tokens are unique and each represents a specific item.

items.translation: a shared, append-only ledger copied across many computers that agree on its contents
items.example: A public blockchain lets anyone download the full history and verify it.

items.translation: a running record of transactions and balances - who owns what
items.example: A bank statement is a familiar everyday example of a ledger.

items.translation: a fixed-size, one-way fingerprint of data that is hard to reverse
items.example: Change one letter of the input and the hash changes completely.

items.translation: a computer running the network's software and usually storing a copy of the ledger
items.example: A full node checks that every incoming block follows the rules.

items.translation: the rules that let distrustful computers agree on one ordered history
items.example: Proof of work and proof of stake are two consensus mechanisms.

items.translation: the secret value that signs transactions and proves control of an address
items.example: Lose your private key and the funds at that address become permanently inaccessible.

items.translation: code stored on a blockchain that runs automatically when triggered
items.example: An escrow smart contract can release funds only after delivery is confirmed.

items.translation: the property that confirmed records are very hard to change after the fact
items.example: Deep transactions gain immutability as more blocks are stacked on top of them.

lessons.title: Beyond currency: use cases, limitations, and the regulatory landscape
lessons.grammar_note: Permissioned blockchains restrict who may read or write; permissionless ones let anyone join - the trade-off is control versus openness.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Give a balanced picture of what blockchains are used for beyond cryptocurrency, where they fall short, and how governments and ethics enter the picture. By the end you will be able to name several non-currency use cases, list the main limitations - scalability, energy, scams, and volatility - and describe key questions regulators are trying to answer. Warm-up: thinking back over the course, name one strength and one weakness of putting records on a permanent, shared ledger. This closing lesson is deliberately even-handed. Blockchains are a genuine engineering tool with real uses, and they are also surrounded by hype, speculation, and outright fraud. A clear-eyed learner should be able to tell a sober use case from a sales pitch, and to explain, without cheerleading or dismissiveness, both what the technology can do and what it cannot. That judgment is the main thing to take away from the whole course.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Away from coins, the common thread in blockchain use cases is a shared record that several parties who do not fully trust each other can all rely on. Supply-chain tracking can record where goods came from so partners see one agreed history. Some registries record ownership or certificates to reduce disputes. Cross-border payments and settlement can, in some designs, move value between institutions faster than older systems. Permissioned blockchains, where a known group controls who can read and write, are often used by businesses that want a shared ledger without a fully public, open network. The honest caveat is that many proposed use cases do not actually need a blockchain; if one trusted party can keep the records, an ordinary database is simpler, cheaper, and faster. A blockchain earns its keep mainly when removing a central keeper is genuinely valuable and no single party can be trusted to hold the record alone. Asking whether that condition truly holds is the first and most important test before reaching for this tool.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: The main limitations are concrete. Scalability: public blockchains process a limited number of transactions per second because every node must verify everything, so fees can spike and confirmation can slow under load; projects address this with second-layer systems and other designs, with mixed results. Energy: proof-of-work networks consume large amounts of electricity by design, which has a real environmental cost, while proof of stake greatly reduces this. Scams and fraud: the same irreversibility that protects honest users also means stolen funds are rarely recoverable, and the field attracts fake projects, rug pulls where founders vanish with investors' money, and exploits of buggy contracts. Volatility: many crypto-assets swing wildly in price, which makes them risky to hold and poor at the everyday job of a stable currency. A balanced reading is that these are not minor bugs to be patched away but structural trade-offs. Decentralization, openness, and irreversibility bring benefits and costs together; you cannot keep only the upside. Treat bold promises of high, guaranteed returns as a warning sign, since no legitimate technology removes financial risk.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What condition makes a blockchain genuinely worth using over a normal database? 2) Name two technical limitations of public blockchains. 3) What is a rug pull? 4) Why is high volatility a problem for a currency? 5) Which consensus approach greatly reduces energy use? Answers: 1) When removing a central keeper is valuable and no single party can be trusted to hold the shared record. 2) Limited scalability (low transactions per second, higher fees under load) and, for proof of work, high energy use. 3) A scam where the creators of a project abruptly withdraw the money and disappear, leaving investors with worthless holdings. 4) A good currency should hold roughly steady value; wild price swings make it hard to price goods, save, or spend reliably. 5) Proof of stake.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming every problem improves with a blockchain. Most record-keeping is served better by a normal database; the blockchain is a specialist tool. Mistake: confusing a public price chart with the health of the underlying technology. Price and usefulness can move independently. Mistake: trusting projects that promise guaranteed or outsized returns; such promises are a classic sign of fraud. On regulation and ethics, the open questions include how to prevent money laundering and protect consumers without crushing useful innovation, how to tax and account for crypto-assets, how to treat stablecoins pegged to national currencies, and how to weigh energy use against claimed benefits. Rules differ sharply by country and keep changing, so what is allowed where you live may differ from what you read online. Exit ticket: (a) Give one real non-currency use case and one honest limitation. (b) Name two questions regulators are wrestling with. Answers: a shared supply-chain or ownership record is a real use case, while scalability, energy, scams, or volatility are honest limitations; regulators are weighing consumer protection and anti-money-laundering rules against innovation, plus how to tax crypto-assets and how to handle stablecoins.
